passages.title: The Piper Plays
passages.text:
Into the street the Piper stept,
Smiling first a little smile,
As if he knew what magic slept
In his quiet pipe the while;
Then, like a musical adept,
To blow the pipe his lips he wrinkled,
And green and blue his sharp eyes twinkled,
Like a candle-flame where salt is sprinkled;
And ere three shrill notes the pipe uttered,
You heard as if an army muttered;
And the muttering grew to a grumbling;
And the grumbling grew to a mighty rumbling;
And out of the houses the rats came tumbling.
Great rats, small rats, lean rats, brawny rats,
Brown rats, black rats, grey rats, tawny rats,
Grave old plodders, gay young friskers,
Fathers, mothers, uncles, cousins,
Cocking tails and pricking whiskers,
Families by tens and dozens,
Brothers, sisters, husbands, wives--
Followed the Piper for their lives.
From street to street he piped advancing,
And step for step they followed dancing,
Until they came to the river Weser
Wherein all plunged and perished!
--Save one who, stout as Julius Caesar,
Swam across and lived to carry
(As he, the manuscript he cherished)
To Rat-land home his commentary:
Which was, "At the first shrill notes of the pipe,
I heard a sound as of scraping tripe,
And putting apples, wondrous ripe,
Into a cider-press's gripe:
And a moving away of pickle-tub-boards,
And a leaving ajar of conserve-cupboards,
And a drawing the corks of train-oil-flasks,
And a breaking the hoops of butter-casks:
And it seemed as if a voice
(Sweeter far than by harp or by psaltery
Is breathed) called out, 'Oh rats, rejoice!
The world is grown to one vast drysaltery!
So munch on, crunch on, take your nuncheon,
Breakfast, supper, dinner, luncheon!'
And just as a bulky sugar-puncheon,
All ready staved, like a great sun shone
Glorious scarce an inch before me,
Just as methought it said, 'Come, bore me!'
--I found the Weser rolling o'er me."

Once more he stept into the street,
And to his lips again
Laid his long pipe of smooth straight cane;
And ere he blew three notes (such sweet
Soft notes as yet musician's cunning
Never gave the enraptured air)
There was a rustling, that seemed like a bustling
Of merry crowds justling at pitching and hustling,
Small feet were pattering, wooden shoes clattering,
Little hands clapping and little tongues chattering,
And, like fowls in a farm-yard when barley is scattering,
Out came the children running.
All the little boys and girls,
With rosy cheeks and flaxen curls,
And sparkling eyes and teeth like pearls,
Tripping and skipping, ran merrily after
The wonderful music with shouting and laughter.
passages.source_note: Public domain: from The Pied Piper of Hamelin by Robert Browning (1842). Straight quotation marks substituted for typographic ones.

questions.stem: As the Piper first entered the street, what did he do before he began to play?

options.text: He shouted a warning to the town
He smiled a small smile
He counted the houses one by one
He tuned the strings of a harp
He knocked upon the Mayor's door

questions.explanation: The poem says he stepped into the street 'Smiling first a little smile', so a small smile came before the music.

questions.stem: The poet writes that the Piper's eyes were 'Like a candle-flame where salt is sprinkled'. What picture does this create of his eyes?

options.text: They were dull and heavy with tiredness
They were cold and completely still
They filled slowly with quiet tears
They flickered with a bright, restless, unnatural light
They were shut tight against the wind

questions.explanation: Salt thrown on a flame makes it flare and spit with sudden colour; the image suggests his eyes flickered with bright, restless, almost unnatural light.

questions.stem: The noise 'grew to a grumbling' and then 'grew to a mighty rumbling'. How does the poet make the sound seem to swell?

options.text: By using a single quiet word only once
By suddenly stopping every sound at once
By describing colours instead of sounds
By asking the reader a direct question
By repeating a rising pattern with steadily heavier words

questions.explanation: By repeating the pattern 'grew to a...' with words that get heavier -- grumbling, then mighty rumbling -- the poet makes the noise seem to build steadily louder.

questions.stem: Words such as 'tumbling', 'muttering' and 'rumbling' share a repeated soft ending. What is this technique, and why does the poet use it here?

options.text: A rhyming couplet that ends the whole stanza neatly
A list of colours used to paint a vivid scene
Echoing endings whose sound imitates the swelling noise itself
A question left deliberately unanswered for effect
A sudden change from past tense into future tense

questions.explanation: Their echoing '-ing' endings and rolling sounds imitate the low, continuous noise of the rats pouring out, so the sound of the words mirrors the sound being described.

questions.stem: Before the rats appear, the poet says 'You heard as if an army muttered'. What does comparing the sound to an army suggest?

options.text: That a vast, threatening crowd was gathering unseen
That soldiers were marching into the town to help
That the sound was faint and easily ignored
That the Piper was frightened of being attacked
That the townsfolk were singing a cheerful song

questions.explanation: An army is huge, massed and threatening, so the comparison warns the reader that a vast, menacing crowd is gathering before a single rat is even seen.

questions.stem: The line 'Great rats, small rats, lean rats, brawny rats' piles up short describing words in a row. What effect does this rushing list create?

options.text: A slow, mournful pace suited to sadness
A fast, crowded rhythm, as if rats swarm out all at once
A calm, orderly feeling of things in their place
A sense that only one lonely rat appears
A pause that lets the reader rest quietly

questions.explanation: The quick, pounding series of paired words gives a fast, crowded rhythm that makes it feel as though rats of every kind are swarming out all at once.

questions.stem: According to the poem, what happened to the rats once they had followed the Piper out of the town?

options.text: They were caught in traps set by the Mayor
They ran back into the empty houses
They scattered into the surrounding fields
They climbed the tower and hid in the bells
They plunged into the river and drowned

questions.explanation: They followed him to the river Weser, 'Wherein all plunged and perished' -- they went into the river and drowned.

questions.stem: One rat 'stout as Julius Caesar' swam across and lived. Why does the poet let this single rat survive?

options.text: To show the Piper's magic had entirely failed
Because the Mayor had secretly rescued it
So there is a witness to report what the music seemed to promise
To prove the river was too shallow to drown in
Because it was the strongest swimmer in the town

questions.explanation: The survivor carries the story home 'To Rat-land', giving the poem a witness who can report what the pipe's music seemed to promise -- so we learn how the rats were tricked.

questions.stem: The Piper prepares to play 'like a musical adept'. What does the word 'adept' mean here?

options.text: A nervous beginner
A highly skilled expert
A tired old man
A travelling stranger
A curious onlooker

questions.explanation: An adept is a highly skilled expert, so the line says the Piper played like a master musician who knew exactly what he was doing.

questions.stem: The surviving rat describes imagining pickle-tubs, conserve-cupboards and butter-casks all opening. Why does the poet include this greedy list?

options.text: To describe what the townsfolk kept in their kitchens
To prove the rats were not really hungry at all
To show how the music tempted the rats with dreams of feasting
To explain how the Piper earned his thousand guilders
To warn the reader against eating too much rich food

questions.explanation: The heap of delicious foods shows how the music tempted the rats by filling their minds with feasting, explaining why they followed so eagerly to their deaths.

questions.stem: The pipe first sounds 'three shrill notes'. What does 'shrill' tell us about these notes?

options.text: They were low and gentle
They were slow and sorrowful
They were faint and almost silent
They were warm and comforting
They were high-pitched and piercing

questions.explanation: 'Shrill' means high-pitched and piercing, so the first notes rang out sharp and sudden rather than soft or deep.

questions.stem: Taken as a whole, this extract tells a story through verse that rhymes and keeps a strong beat. What kind of poem does this make it?

options.text: A limerick, a short comic poem of exactly five lines
A haiku, an unrhymed poem of seventeen syllables
A narrative poem, which tells a story in rhythmic, rhyming verse
An acrostic, in which the first letters spell a word
A shape poem, whose lines are arranged to form a picture

questions.explanation: It relates a sequence of events -- the Piper plays, the creatures gather, they follow to the river -- in rhymed, rhythmic lines, which is exactly what a narrative poem does: it tells a tale in verse.

questions.stem: The extract shows the Piper playing on two separate occasions. How are these two parts of the poem shaped in relation to each other?

options.text: The second echoes the first, but the young follow instead of rats
The second contradicts and cancels out the first entirely
The two parts describe the very same moment twice over
The second explains a mystery left open in the first
The two parts have nothing in common with each other

questions.explanation: The second playing deliberately echoes the first -- he steps into the street and lifts his pipe again -- but this time children rather than rats follow, so the structure repeats the pattern with a chilling change.

questions.stem: As the children rush out, the poet writes of 'feet were pattering, wooden shoes clattering' and 'tongues chattering'. What do these rhyming, tapping words help the reader to do?

options.text: Picture the children standing perfectly still and silent
Almost hear the busy, hurrying bustle as they rush out
Understand exactly how far the children had to run
Learn the names of each of the children
Feel the sadness of the watching Mayor

questions.explanation: The light, rhyming '-attering' words tap along like quick footsteps and chatter, letting the reader almost hear the busy, hurrying noise of the crowd of children.

questions.stem: The children are described as having 'teeth like pearls'. Which technique is the poet using in this phrase?

options.text: A rhetorical question
An exaggeration for comic effect
A pair of rhyming words
A repeated opening word
A simile

questions.explanation: Because it compares two different things using the word 'like' -- teeth and pearls -- the phrase is a simile.

questions.stem: How does the poem describe the appearance of the little boys and girls who come running?

options.text: With pale faces and dark hair
In ragged, dirty clothing
Wearing heavy winter coats
Carrying baskets of bread
With rosy cheeks and fair curls

questions.explanation: They are pictured 'With rosy cheeks and flaxen curls', that is, with pink cheeks and fair, golden hair.

questions.stem: When the children follow, they run 'merrily after' the music 'with shouting and laughter'. What mood does the poet create at this point, and why is it unsettling?

options.text: A joyful mood that is unsettling because we fear where they are led
A gloomy mood that matches the children's sadness
An angry mood as the children protest loudly
A calm, sleepy mood in which nothing much happens
A puzzled mood because the children do not understand music

questions.explanation: The poet makes the children sound joyful and carefree, yet the reader already knows the pipe led the rats to drown -- so the happy mood makes the danger feel far more disturbing.

questions.stem: Nothing in the extract stops the children as they stream out of the houses and away. What does this suggest about the power the Piper's music holds?

options.text: The music has an irresistible, magical pull nothing can resist
The children have simply chosen to go for an ordinary walk
The parents have arranged the outing in advance
The Piper is forcing the children along against loud protest
The music is so quiet only a few children can hear it

questions.explanation: The children pour out and follow the moment the pipe sounds, with no one able to hold them back, implying the music has an irresistible, magical pull that overrides everything else.

questions.stem: The second tune fills the 'enraptured air' with sound. What does 'enraptured' suggest about the air, or those in it?

options.text: Torn apart by a violent storm
Emptied of every sound at once
Frozen solid by bitter cold
Charmed and spellbound with delight
Choked with thick grey smoke

questions.explanation: 'Enraptured' means filled with delight or spellbound, so the phrase suggests everything around is charmed and enchanted by the beautiful music.

questions.stem: The rat's glowing report ends abruptly: 'I found the Weser rolling o'er me.' What does this sudden final image do to the mood of its speech?

options.text: It carries the cheerful mood on smoothly to the very end
It shows the rat safely reaching the far bank at last
It proves the river was only a picture in the rat's mind
It shatters the bright vision with the cold reality of drowning
It repeats the earlier list of foods one more time

questions.explanation: The line breaks off the rat's blissful vision with the plain, heavy fact of water closing over it, so the glowing picture collapses at once into the cold reality of drowning.

questions.stem: Much of the first section is given over to the surviving rat's own spoken report of what it heard. What does letting the rat speak add to the poem?

options.text: It lists the names of every rat in the town
It explains the rules the Piper must follow
It lets the reader feel the temptation from the inside
It describes the weather on the day of the drowning
It tells the reader how the poem will end happily

questions.explanation: Switching to the rat's first-hand account lets the reader experience the music's temptation from the inside, making the trickery vivid rather than merely described from outside.

questions.stem: At the start the magic is said to sleep in the Piper's 'quiet pipe'. Why is the pipe called 'quiet' at this moment?

options.text: It has not yet been played, so it is still silent
It is broken and can no longer make a sound
It is playing a soft and soothing lullaby
It is far away and can barely be heard
It is being kept hidden inside his coat

questions.explanation: The pipe is 'quiet' because it has not yet been played -- its magic is still asleep and silent until he blows the first notes.

questions.stem: The Piper begins 'As if he knew what magic slept' in his pipe. What does this line suggest about how the Piper feels as he starts?

options.text: Terrified that his plan is about to fail
Bored and reluctant to play at all
Confused about how his own pipe works
Quietly confident, sure his music will do as he intends
Sad that he must leave the town so soon

questions.explanation: Knowing what magic waits in his pipe, the Piper is quietly confident and sure of his power, expecting the music to work exactly as he intends.

questions.stem: The children come out 'like fowls in a farm-yard when barley is scattering'. What does this comparison suggest about how they answer the music?

options.text: They creep out slowly, one nervous child at a time
They refuse to leave the safety of their homes
They march out in neat, orderly rows
They rush out at once, eagerly and without thinking
They come only because their parents drive them

questions.explanation: Hens rush eagerly and all together the instant grain is thrown down, so the image shows the children hurrying out at once, greedily and without thinking, the moment the music calls.

questions.stem: Why might the poet describe the rats being led away in full before he shows the very same trick working on the children?

options.text: So the reader forgets what happened to the rats
So the reader already dreads the fate now facing the children
To prove the Piper has changed his mind and turned kind
To show that the children are safer than the rats were
To fill space before the real story begins

questions.explanation: By first showing exactly how the music lured the rats to drown, the poet makes the reader dread the identical fate now hanging over the children, so the second scene fills us with alarm.
